newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: FEATURE - Tajik town caught in civil war's crossfire.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Tajik town caught in civil war's crossfire.

text.p: Izatullo Khalimov, chief administrator in the Tajik town of Komsomolabad, sat down behind an empty desk, took a deep breath and, staring at his hands, unloaded his troubles.

Guerrillas from the Islamist opposition, which have waged war against the Tajik government for nearly five years, swooped on the town in October and disarmed and imprisoned Khalimov's local security force.
The guerrillas later released some police officers but Khalimov had yet to learn the fate of the town's prosecutor and the security ministry's local representative.
Nor did he know how he was going to find the flour and fuel needed to sustain the Komsomolabad district's 65,000 population through the coming winter.

Ice had begun to form over the streams. The slim grey poplars were bare of leaves. Young girls, in livid green, red and orange dresses darted like parakeets between the houses on the muddy, wintry streets.
Khalimov said relief agencies were not prepared to risk delivering aid to the war-torn region.

In a worn suit and carefully maintaining the tacky trappings of the Soviet bureaucrat he once was, Khalimov looked out of place in the small town, dwarfed by the surrounding Vakhsh mountain range 170 km (100 miles) east of the capital Dushanbe.

A portrait of embattled Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov hung behind his desk in place of Vladimir Lenin, a somewhat rash idea in the face of the guerrillas who swaggered about Komsomolabad looking like extras from a spaghetti western.
The bank of telephones next to his desk, once the symbol of power for Soviet-era bureaucrats, went dead in February.
SUPPLIES TO TOWN CUT OFF

Government pilots are too scared of opposition guns to fly their helicopters with supplies and cash to the town and Komsomolabad's last link to Dushanbe is a treacherous mountain road prone to mud slides.
"The administration is working," said Khalimov bravely.
"It is very difficult of course with no militia, no salaries and it is of course unpleasant that the guerrillas carry arms. We are caught between two fronts."

Tajikistan's civil war has claimed around 40,000 lives and made many more homeless. It casts a deathly shadow over most towns and villages in the former Soviet republic, which borders China and Afghanistan.
At a checkpoint at the entrance to the town, guerrilla commander Eshon Saboyev stated baldly: "There is no real power besides us."
Truck drivers, wearing blue embroidered skull caps and driving through Komsomolabad loaded with apples to sell in Dushanbe, approached the armed fighters at the checkpoint with marked respect.

Saboyev, a white bandana tied around his head and an amulet containing verses from the Koran hanging from his neck, was relaxed, but his wolf-like eyes darted instinctively up the road and around the mountain tops.
A pair of falcons wheeled on warm updrafts above the iron-red Vakhsh River which flowed past the town.

Saboyev would not say why his men had allowed Khalimov to carry on working. Like Khalimov himself, the fighters appeared to be waiting for the outcome of planned peace talks on December 9 between Rakhmonov and opposition leader Sayid Abdullo Nuri.
LITTLE STORE SET BY NEGOTIATIONS

A tangled web of regional and clan rivalries underpins the nominally ideological struggle between the Islamist guerrillas and the secular government, both fighting for control of the country of 5.7 million people.
Previous negotiations this year only inflamed the fighting, as each side manoeuvred to cement their gains. A United Nations-sponsored ceasefire has been routinely ignored.
"I think these will be the last negotiations. "Either they work," said Saboyev "or we advance."
Gulniso, 15 and wearing an orange dress over red leggings, watched a flock of black sheep on a rock-strewn hillside above the town. She was in no doubt as to who controlled Komsomolabad.
"The opposition controls the town," she said. Nearby, "Allah Akhbar!", or "God is great!", had been daubed on a concrete sign announcing Komsomolabad.
"It was better when the government was here," she added, modestly pulling a scarf across her face. "There was flour then."
